prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: Vikram is / very stronger / than / I am.
explanation: 'Very' cannot modify a comparative; use 'much stronger' (or 'far stronger') than I am.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: He is faster enough / to defeat / the current record holder.
explanation: The 'enough' structure takes the positive degree, not the comparative: 'He is fast enough to defeat...'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: Can you not / knock so louder / in the morning?
explanation: With 'so' the positive degree is required, and the verb needs an adverb: 'knock so loudly' (or 'so loud').

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: My mother is thirty-four (1) / but I am nearly (2) / as taller as her already. (3) / No error (4)
explanation: The 'as...as' construction requires the positive degree, so 'as taller as her' should be 'as tall as her/she'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: He is as smart (1) / if not smarter (2) / than his elder brother. (3) / No error (4)
explanation: The 'as' comparison is left incomplete; it should read 'He is as smart as, if not smarter than, his elder brother.'

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: He was (a) / enough wise (b) / to do the difficult work, (c) / No error (d)
explanation: 'Enough' follows the adjective it modifies, so 'enough wise' should be 'wise enough'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: He is (a) / so respectful (b) / as Gandhiji. (c) / no error (d)
explanation: Equality is expressed with 'as...as', not 'so...as' in affirmative sentences, so it should be 'as respectful as Gandhiji'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: The poor man (a) / was too weaker (b) / to do the work on time, (c) / no error (d)
options: to do the work on time,
explanation: The 'too...to' structure needs the positive degree, so 'too weaker' should be 'too weak'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: Throughout the whole year (a)/ there was not a single day (b)/ without some violence, (c)/ no error (d)
options: there was not a single day
explanation: 'Throughout' already means 'during the whole of', so 'whole' is redundant; write 'Throughout the year' or 'During the whole year'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: Many people don't hardly know (a)/ about the real factors (b)/ that have led the state to so many crises. (c)/ no error (d)
options: that have led the state to so many crises
explanation: 'Hardly' is already negative in sense, so 'don't hardly' is a double negative; it should be 'Many people hardly know'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: She reimbursed back the money which I had (a)/ spent during our (b)/ journey to Kathmandu, (c)/ no error (d)
options: She reimbursed back the money which I had
explanation: 'Reimburse' means to pay back, so 'back' is redundant; write 'She reimbursed the money which I had...'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: The last project of (a)/ the company was (b)/ equally as successful as the first project, (c)/ no error (d)
options: equally as successful as the first project
explanation: 'Equally' and 'as...as' express the same comparison, so combining them is redundant; use 'as successful as the first project' or 'equally successful'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: He is rich enough (A) / to buy a premium luxury apartment (B) / in the most expensive locality of metropolitan Mumbai. (C) / No Error (D)
options: to buy a premium luxury apartment
in the most expensive locality of metropolitan Mumbai.
explanation: No error; 'adjective + enough + to-infinitive' ('rich enough to buy') is the correct pattern.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: The examination was so difficult (A) / that I was only able to solve (B) / two questions completely during the test. (C) / No Error (D)
options: that I was only able to solve
two questions completely during the test.
explanation: 'Only' is misplaced — it must stand before the word it limits: 'that I was able to solve only two questions'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: He is too intelligent (A) / to not understand the hidden implications (B) / behind the diplomat's carefully worded statement. (C) / No Error (D)
options: to not understand the hidden implications
behind the diplomat's carefully worded statement.
explanation: The infinitive should not be split by 'not'; the correct idiom is 'too intelligent not to understand'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: He is as intelligent, (A) / if not more intelligent than, (B) / his elder brother who works at NASA. (C) / No Error (D)
options: his elder brother who works at NASA.
explanation: The double comparison needs both halves complete: 'as intelligent as, if not more intelligent than'. Part (A) drops the second 'as', so it should read 'He is as intelligent as,'.

sentence: Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains a grammatical error. If you don’t find any error, mark ‘No error’ as your answer. Her concerts / are very admired / by the foreigners / no error.
explanation: Past participles used with verbs of feeling take 'much/greatly', not 'very': 'are much admired'.

sentence: Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains a grammatical error. Bobo was / very richer than Jim / as he had illicitly accumulated / all his wealth.
explanation: A comparative degree is intensified by 'much' or 'far', not 'very'; it should be 'much richer than Jim'.

sentence: Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error. Rahul thinks he is as smarter as his friends in the class.
explanation: The 'as...as' construction takes the positive degree, so it must be 'as smart as', not 'as smarter as'.

prompt: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
sentence: My dog / barks / very louder / at night.
explanation: 'Very' cannot modify a comparative, and the verb 'barks' needs an adverb: 'very loudly' (or 'much louder').

prompt: Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.
sentence: Aren’t you such young to travel by yourself?
explanation: Before an adjective + infinitive, 'too' is used, not 'such'; it should be 'too young to travel'.

prompt: Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, then select the option "No error".
sentence: A witness had seen a youth, / perhaps aged young as/ ten or eleven, acting suspiciously.
options: A witness had seen a youth
explanation: The comparison of equality needs the 'as ... as' structure: 'perhaps as young as ten or eleven'.

prompt: The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don’t find any error, mark ‘No error’ as your answer.
sentence: The food container / is not enough big to meet / the demands of the affected people.
options: is not enough big to meet
the demands of the affected people.
explanation: 'Enough' follows the adjective it modifies, so the correct form is 'is not big enough to meet'.

sentence: Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error. The news is very good to be true.
explanation: The idiomatic structure is 'too + adjective + to + verb', so it must be 'too good to be true'; 'very' cannot be used with the 'to-infinitive' of excess.

prompt: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. Since the little girl answers / a few simple questions, / her parents say that / she is too intelligent.
explanation: 'Too' implies excess with a negative result; praising the girl requires 'very intelligent'.

prompt: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
sentence: The hotel room, / which we / booked, / isn’t enough big.
explanation: 'Enough' follows the adjective it modifies, so the correct form is 'isn't big enough'.

prompt: Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.
sentence: Do you earn so much to make both ends meet?
explanation: To express sufficiency the structure is 'enough to', so 'so much to make both ends meet' should be 'enough to make both ends meet'.

prompt: Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.
sentence: He is / too immature / for handle / the situation.
explanation: The structure 'too + adjective' is followed by an infinitive, so 'for handle' must be 'to handle'.

prompt: The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don’t find any error, mark ‘No error’ as your answer.
sentence: He was enough tall / to be admitted / into the armed forces.
explanation: 'Enough' follows the adjective it modifies: 'tall enough to be admitted'.

sentence: Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don’t find any error, mark ‘No error’ as your answer. Everything happened such quickly that I felt dazed.
explanation: Before an adverb/adjective we use 'so ... that', not 'such ... that': 'so quickly that'.

prompt: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
sentence: He entered the room / such quietly that / none of us / noticed him.
explanation: 'So' (not 'such') is used before an adverb, giving 'so quietly that'.

prompt: Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose “No error’.
sentence: Producing a different component was as simple such launching a new computer program.
explanation: The comparison of equality requires 'as simple as', not 'as simple such'; 'such' cannot introduce the second term of an as...as comparison.

prompt: Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select "No error’.
sentence: I have never seen a man / get off his horse quick as / did that stranger Englishman.
options: No error 4 get off his horse quick as
explanation: The equality comparison needs 'as quickly as' — an adverb to modify 'get off' plus the first 'as'; 'quick as' is wrong.

sentence: Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error. Vikram is very stronger than I am.
explanation: 'Very' cannot modify a comparative adjective; 'much stronger' (or 'far stronger') is required.

prompt: The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don’t find any error, mark ‘No error’ as your answer.
sentence: Her decision, / given the complex circumstances, / was too impulsively made.
explanation: After the linking verb 'was' an adjective is needed, and 'too' requires a completing clause, so it should be 'was very impulsive'.

prompt: The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don’t find any error, mark ‘No error’ as your answer.
sentence: She is / as more intelligent as / her brothers are.
explanation: The 'as ... as' structure takes the positive degree, so it should be 'as intelligent as', not 'as more intelligent as'.

sentence: Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error. I have never seen so beautiful a landscape than this one.
explanation: 'So ... as' is the correct correlative in a negative comparison: 'so beautiful a landscape as this one'.

sentence: Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains a grammatical error. Ms. Malathi is old much to join a college now.
explanation: The intensifier must precede the adjective in the 'too + adjective + to + verb' pattern, so 'old much' should be 'too old'.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given
sentence: If no substitution is required, select No improvement. His school was 7 km away from his house. I wondered how he covered so long distance daily on foot.
explanation: With a singular countable noun plus adjective, 'such a long distance' is the correct structure ('so long a distance' would also be valid).

prompt: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given
sentence: If no substitution is required, select No improvement. The Head has been so busy to go through these files and resolve the matter.
options: too so busy to go through
explanation: 'Too + adjective + to + verb' expresses an excess preventing an action; 'so' requires a 'that' clause.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given
sentence: If no substitution is required, select No improvement. We had never seen so strong blizzard. The wind speed was 130 km per hour .
explanation: With a singular countable noun, the structure is 'such a strong blizzard' (or 'so strong a blizzard').

prompt: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given
sentence: If no substitution is required, select No improvement. Each dancer performed very well that it was difficult to judge who the best was.
explanation: 'So + adverb + that' is the correct correlative structure; 'such' cannot modify the adverb 'well'.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given
sentence: If no substitution is required, select No improvement. She was so tired to work any longer.
explanation: The 'too + adjective + to + verb' structure expresses excess; 'so' would require 'that'.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution required’.
sentence: She was too startled at first saying something , but finally she blurted out the truth.
explanation: 'Too + adjective' is completed by an infinitive, and the negative sense of 'too startled' requires 'any' — 'too startled at first to say anything'.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select No improvement.
sentence: Frost occurs in the northern part of the state as frequently than in the central part.
explanation: 'Than' requires the comparative form, so 'as frequently than' must become 'more frequently than'; 'as...as' and 'more...than' cannot be mixed.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution required’.
sentence: The song was so moving as all eyes became wet.
explanation: The correlative for degree and result is 'so ... that', not 'so ... as' in an affirmative sentence.

prompt: Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case
sentence: no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'. Is this the same book like our teacher recommended?
explanation: 'The same' is always followed by 'as', never by 'like', when introducing a clause of comparison.

prompt: Identify the best way to improve the underlined part of the given sentence. If there is no
sentence: improvement required, select ‘no improvement’. She is a very good sprinter. I can’t run as fast as she does.
explanation: The comparison 'as fast as she does' is correct, with 'does' properly substituting for the verb 'runs'.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option to improve the underlined segment in the given
sentence: If there is no need to improve it, select ‘No improvement’. She was so tall to reach the top shelf.
explanation: 'So ... to' is wrong; the structure showing sufficiency is 'adjective + enough + to + verb', so 'tall enough to reach' is correct.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
sentence: Planets in our solar system close and big for them to twinkle.
explanation: The sentence needs a finite plural verb and the 'too + adjective + for + object + to-infinitive' structure expressing a negative result.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
sentence: He has recovered now and is feeling too strong to walk.
explanation: Since he has recovered, the positive sense requires 'strong enough to walk'; 'too...to' conveys a negative result.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
sentence: Mahima is as smarter as Shilpi.
explanation: The 'as ... as' construction of equality requires the positive degree, so 'as smart as' is correct.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
sentence: Please take many as you want.
explanation: 'Take' with the uncountable/indefinite quantity here needs the correlative 'as much as': 'Please take as much as you want.'

prompt: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution required’.
sentence: The exam was not so easy that we had expected.
explanation: Comparison of equality/degree requires the 'as ... as' structure: 'not as easy as we had expected'.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘no substitution required’,
sentence: Some of them were nearly (as hard as ligament. and many an inch in length).
options: hard as ligament, and many an inch at length
as hard as a ligament, and many an inches in length
explanation: 'As hard as ligament' correctly uses the as...as construction and 'many an inch' correctly follows 'many a/an' with a singular noun, so no substitution is required.

prompt: Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose ‘No improvement’ as an answer if the sentence is grammatically comect.
sentence: The dessert was many sweet for my tastes.
explanation: 'Many' cannot intensify an adjective; the degree adverb 'too' is required before 'sweet' — 'too sweet for my taste'.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
sentence: The food was too salty eat this morning.
explanation: The structure is 'too + adjective + to + V1': 'too salty to eat'.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
sentence: A raven, which you know is black as coal, was envious of the swan, because her feathers are as white as the purest snow.
explanation: The plural subject 'feathers' needs 'were' to match the past-tense narration, and the comparison of equality is 'as white as'.
